titre: Twelve Years Tracking a Whale No One Has Ever Seen
accroche: Since 1989, military hydrophones in the North Pacific have picked up the song of a whale that no other whale ever seems to join.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1989, U.S. Navy analysts spot an unusual song in the North Pacific, picked up by the SOSUS hydrophone network, designed during the Cold War to detect Soviet submarines. The sound repeats, season after season, at a frequency of 50 to 52 hertz, markedly higher than the deep rumble typical of the large baleen whales that share these waters. The analysts attribute it to a whale, without being able to say which one.

## Twelve Years of Acoustic Shadowing

The signal had already been heard intermittently as early as 1989. But its systematic tracking did not begin until 1992, once part of the SOSUS data was declassified at the end of the Cold War. A team from the Woods Hole oceanographic institution, led by the bioacoustician William Watkins, then sets out to follow this signal's trail, with a monitoring program that continues without interruption from 1995. For twelve years, the same song reappears every season, between August and February, without ever overlapping with a second identical signal. Everything indicates that a single source is responsible, one and the same whale followed from year to year. Its tracks, measured by triangulation between several arrays spread across the ocean, vary from 708 to 11,062 kilometers depending on the season, covered at a speed of 0.7 to 3.8 kilometers per hour. In 2004, Watkins and his colleagues publish the synthesis of this tracking of fifteen years of recordings. Their conclusion fits in one sentence: the species producing these calls remains unknown.

## An Animal Never Seen, a Loneliness Never Proven

Watkins dies in September 2004, a few weeks before the online publication of this article, without ever having seen the animal he had followed for more than a decade. No one has done better since: no capture, no genetic sample, no photograph has made it possible to identify the species, or even to confirm whether it is an isolated individual, a hybrid between two known species, or a vocal malformation in an otherwise ordinary whale.

The nickname "the world's loneliest whale," which made it popular, therefore tells less of an established fact than of a projection: what the hydrophones prove is that no second identical song was ever picked up at the same time, not that the animal is deprived of company. It could just as well be swimming among other whales, in a register they simply do not hear.

carte.punch: A whale has been singing since 1989, and no one knows what species it belongs to.
carte.idee: Tracked by military hydrophones in the North Pacific for twelve years, this whale emits a 52-hertz song that no second identical signal has ever corroborated. Its species remains unknown, and its nickname of “the world's loneliest whale” remains unproven.

quiz.question: Why do the Woods Hole researchers think the 52-hertz calls come from one and the same whale, year after year?
choix: Because a transmitter was attached to the animal during a capture in 1989
Because divers photographed the same individual on several occasions
Because no second identical signal was ever picked up at the same time as the first
Because geneticists compared DNA collected from seawater
quiz.explication: The tracking rests on listening, not on observation: the SOSUS network's hydrophones never recorded two series of 52-hertz calls at the same time in twelve years, which indicates a single source. No capture, genetic sample, or photograph has ever been made of this animal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: For what purpose had the SOSUS hydrophone network, which made it possible to detect the 52-hertz song, been designed?
choix: To study the migration of large baleen whales
To detect Soviet submarines during the Cold War
To measure ocean temperature at great depth
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The SOSUS network had been designed during the Cold War to detect Soviet submarines; it was only after a partial declassification in 1992 that its tracking of the whale could begin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: At what frequency is the song the researchers tracked, and how does it compare with that of other large whales?
choix: 50 to 52 hertz, markedly higher than the deep rumble typical of baleen whales
5 to 8 hertz, much deeper than that of other whales
50 to 52 hertz, exactly identical to that of blue whales
200 to 250 hertz, a frequency inaudible to other whales
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The signal repeats at a frequency of 50 to 52 hertz, markedly higher than the deep rumble typical of the large baleen whales that share the same waters.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What prevented William Watkins from publishing the synthesis of his whale tracking himself?
choix: A refusal by Deep-Sea Research to publish his results
The loss of part of the recordings in a storm
His death in September 2004, a few weeks before the online publication of the article
The decommissioning of the SOSUS program before his analysis was finished
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Watkins dies in September 2004, a few weeks before the online publication of the synthesis article, without ever having seen the animal he had followed for more than a decade.
